newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba-fixed repo valued during uncertain periods.
newsitem.headline: Buba-fixed repo valued during uncertain periods.

text.p: The German Bundesbank said on Tuesday that fixed rate securities repurchase agreements were most valuable during periods of interest rate uncertainty such as now.

The central bank said in its monthly report for November that the choice of monetary policy instruments influenced capital market interest rates mainly during times of increasing uncertainty. It added a fixed rate repo provided the clearest indication about the central bank's monetary leanings.
"This form (a fixed rate repo) of central bank money gives clear interest rate guidelines which lead the market and avoid undesired fluctuations in money and capital market rates," the bank said.

"At the end of 1993, during the climbing yields of 1994 or since the start of the year, the Bundesbank has preferred to use a fixed tender during its weekly securities repurchase operations," the report said.
Economists broadly agree the Bundesbank will keep interest rates on hold for the rest of the year. But they remain unsure whether the bank will lift or reduce rates the next time it adjusts policy.

The Bundesbank, which has kept the securities repurchase rate, or repo, fixed at 3.00 percent since August, has given few hints about its monetary leanings of late, with several council members saying that there was no need to adjust interest rates.
The central bank report also offered the by now familar warnings about the dangers of entering into monetary union if the fiscal health of participants is not sound.
The report said a politically-driven convergence of interest rates among European nations should not replace a convergence of fundamental factors.
"It would be a heavy mortgage for the credability of EMU monetary policy," the Bundesbank said of confusing political and economic reasons for yield convergence.

The bank expressed disappointment that the difference between long- and short-term interest rates had remained large, saying the wide spread was in part due to expectations about European monetary union.
According to monetary union time-tables, long-term German bonds would be repaid in Euro's, not the traditionally strong mark.

The Bundesbank said the steep yield curve reflected the view that "uncertainty or scepticism about interest and inflation rates is connected to European monetary union," adding there worries were most pronounced regarding fiscal convergence.
It said attempts at "creative accounting" of the fiscal criteria were increasingly being viewed critically.
